source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Blind expert review found LLM ideas rated more novel than expert-written ideas, with similar scores on most other metrics.
numbers: Novelty mean 4.84 (human, 49 ideas) vs 5.64 (AI) vs 5.81 (AI + human rerank); 79 reviewers; Welch t-test with Bonferroni, p<0.01 treating each review as a datapoint (109 reviews per condition). Feasibility not significantly different.
limits: Idea-stage review only, no execution. One topic family (NLP prompting). Human ideas were written by experts in limited time and often not their best idea.
agent_relevance: Novelty is the one metric where the model wins, and it is the metric judged most subjectively. Treat a novelty gain on idea text as unproven until executed.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Expert reviewers disagree with each other on idea quality. Human-human agreement on top/bottom 25% ranking was barely above chance.
numbers: Inter-reviewer balanced accuracy 56.1% (random 50%). Reference points: NeurIPS 2021 reviewers 66.0%, ICLR 2024 LLM-topic submissions 71.9%. Split-half over reviewers, 20 random splits.
limits: Metric is balanced accuracy on top/bottom quartile, not Krippendorff alpha (reviews did not overlap enough). Idea-only review is more subjective than reviewing executed papers.
agent_relevance: Human raters of ideas are a noisy gold standard. Any check of our novelty measure against a small rated set must report rater noise first.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: LLM judges of ideas did not beat the human reliability baseline. Every tested evaluator was at or below human-human agreement, several near chance.
numbers: Accuracy vs mean expert score on top/bottom 25%: GPT-4o direct 50.0, GPT-4o pairwise 45.0, Claude-3.5 direct 51.7, Claude-3.5 pairwise 53.3, AI-Scientist reviewer 43.3, vs human-human 56.1. The same pairwise ranker got 71.4% on ICLR accept/reject pairs (GPT-4o 61.1, Claude-3-Opus 63.5); few-shot and CoT gave no significant gain there.
quote: All of these LLM evaluators have a lower agreement than our expert reviewers' scores.
limits: Ideas all on similar NLP topics, which makes ranking harder. Authors warn that matching human agreement would not prove validity: the model may trade variance for bias.
agent_relevance: Supports G5 and G8: do not let a model judge pick the novel idea. Judge skill measured on paper accept/reject does not transfer to idea novelty.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Generating many ideas from one model hits a diversity ceiling: most samples are near-duplicates, so sample count is a poor proxy for coverage.
numbers: Of 4000 generated seed ideas per topic, only about 200 were non-duplicates (about 5%) at cosine similarity 0.8 on all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings; the accumulated non-duplicates plateau.
limits: Threshold 0.8 chosen by manual inspection. Depends on one embedding model and one generation prompt.
agent_relevance: Open mode: dedupe in code with an embedding threshold and count distinct ideas, not drafts. A cheap code-run diversity measure.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: The agent's own ranker and the expert reranking disagree, so the agent's top picks are not the human's top picks.
numbers: Only 17 of the 49 ideas in the AI + Human Rerank condition overlap with the AI-ranked condition (Table 12). Ranker was Claude-3.5-Sonnet zero-shot pairwise with Swiss-system tournament; ICLR proxy: top-10 vs bottom-10 gap in review score 0.56 to 1.73 over 1 to 6 rounds.
limits: Reranking was done by one person (first author).
agent_relevance: Self-ranking of own ideas is weak signal. Use code-based selection on checks, not model preference.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang et al. (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Human Research Ideas
finding: Executing the same ideas erased the LLM novelty advantage. 43 experts spent 100+ hours each implementing assigned ideas; scores of LLM ideas dropped more than those of human ideas on every metric.
numbers: Execution time averaged 112.6 h (human ideas) and 93.7 h (AI ideas); reviewers spent 52.5 min per paper. Drop larger for LLM ideas on novelty, excitement, effectiveness and overall (p<0.05). Per-review test (N=181): human ideas higher on excitement, effectiveness, soundness, overall, not novelty. Per-idea test (N=43; 19 human, 24 AI): no significant difference on any metric.
limits: Preregistered hypothesis not confirmed at per-idea power. Executors changed ideas (metrics, hyper-parameters). Reviewers saw a 4-page paper, not long-term impact. NLP only.
agent_relevance: This is the validated alternative to judging: score a candidate by what happens when it is executed. For our agent: run candidates against held-out checks, not how novel they read (G3).

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang et al. (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Human Research Ideas
finding: Idea-stage scores predict execution-stage scores poorly. The ideation score had almost no correlation with the later score of the same idea.
numbers: Appendix D: AI ideas Pearson r novelty -0.019, excitement -0.321, effectiveness 0.172, overall -0.092; Spearman excitement -0.386. Human ideas r novelty -0.084, excitement 0.205, effectiveness 0.022, overall 0.158.
quote: The correlation is weak in most cases; for AI ideas, there is even a moderately negative correlation on the excitement score.
limits: Small N per condition (19 and 24 ideas). Restricted range likely lowers r. Reviewers differ between stages.
agent_relevance: Perceived novelty at proposal time is not a reliable selection criterion. Prefer pass/fail on executed output.

source: Schopf and Farber (2026) Is this Idea Novel? An Automated Benchmark for Judgment of Research Ideas (RINoBench)
finding: Benchmark of 1,381 research ideas from ICLR 2022/2023 submissions with expert novelty scores 1-5. All tested LLMs, reasoning ones too, judged novelty poorly even when given the related works.
numbers: Macro-F1 over 5 classes at most 17.2 (GPT-5), o3 16.2, GPT-OSS-120B 13.0, Llama-3.1-8B about 12; F1 for class 1 was 0.0 for every model; MAE about 0.93-1.04. Reasoning models only slightly better than non-reasoning. Test split about 277 ideas.
limits: Gold labels come from reviewer text converted to scores by an LLM pipeline (GPT-OSS-120B), so the gold is model-derived. Related works are the paper's own citations.
agent_relevance: Models give plausible reasons but wrong scores. Never gate on a model's novelty score; ask it for evidence and let code compare it.

source: Schopf and Farber (2026) RINoBench
finding: Justification text from LLMs is close to human reasoning even though the scores are not, and mostly grounded.
numbers: Alignment with gold justification roughly 78 to 90 on Known and Novelty aspects (GPT-4.1 as metric judge); hallucination rate about 0.2 to 4.2%.
limits: Justification metrics themselves use an LLM (GPT-4.1).
agent_relevance: The model can extract aspects of overlap with prior work; the verdict step is where it fails. Split extraction (model) from verdict (code).

source: Schopf, Schreieder, Aizawa (2026) Think-Probe-Respond: Improving LLMs as Judges of Research Idea Novelty
finding: Model judges have a systematic bias to the middle: they say medium novelty even when their reasoning supports another verdict. Probing hidden states with a trained classifier fixes part of it.
numbers: Best prompted proprietary model macro-F1 only 17.1. TPR (logistic regression on hidden states at the last thinking token, frozen LLM) beat the best competitor by 22.30% on average; chain-of-thought gave marginal gain for non-reasoning models and inconsistent gain for reasoning models.
limits: Needs open-weight models with hidden-state access. Trained on the RINoBench train split, so in-distribution. Same noisy gold as c08.
agent_relevance: Telling a model to think step by step does not fix miscalibrated novelty. Calibration in code (class priors, a probe) matters more than prompt wording. Hidden states are not available to a prompt-only scaffold.

source: Sinhahajari, Majumder, Poria (2026) On the Limits of LLM-as-Judge for Scientific Novelty Assessment (RQ-Bench)
finding: Novelty mirage: LLM judges rate model-written research questions as more novel than the questions real authors pursued, while experts prefer the author questions.
numbers: 50 sampled pairs from cs.CL and cs.LG, best-of-five gpt-5.5 RQ vs author-anchored RQ, blinded experts on non-obviousness. Experts preferred the author RQ with win rates 78% and 56%. LLM judges favoured the model RQ: 82% (gemini-3.1-pro) and 52% (deepseek-v4-pro). Human-LLM agreement as low as 22%; expert-expert 60%, LLM-LLM 52%.
quote: LLM judges consistently rate model-generated RQs as highly novel, producing a novelty mirage
limits: Only 50 items, two experts, two LLM judges. The author RQ is a reference, not the only valid question. Authors say novelty is partly subjective.
agent_relevance: Same-family bias risk: a model judging model output over-credits it (G5, G8). Use an external reference set and a human anchor, not the model.

source: Sinhahajari et al. (2026) RQ-Bench
finding: Pairwise (comparative) judging made the bias worse, because the judge is forced to break ties toward the model output.
numbers: gpt-5.5 strict win rate on non-obviousness rose from 27.2% (standalone, two judges combined) to 49.1% (comparative); tie rate fell from 59.1% to 36.8%. Standalone originality win rate 38.4%.
limits: Win rates depend on two judge models and the authors' rubric.
agent_relevance: Pairwise comparison is not a safe fix for rating inflation. In our selector, allow ties and require evidence for a win.

source: Sinhahajari et al. (2026) RQ-Bench
finding: When judges were told to test one extra dimension, narrowness or source-boundedness, their verdicts moved toward the experts. The missing rubric dimension was the gap.
numbers: Experts flagged generated RQs as narrow and tied to the background. With an explicit narrowness test, model RQs lost to the reference 71.7% of the time standalone (won 4.3%); under comparative judging the lose rate rose to 85.4%. Diagnostic framing lose rate 2.9% to 53.4%.
limits: Same small benchmark; the rubric was added after seeing the failure, so it may be fitted to it.
agent_relevance: A rubric that names the failure (generic, bound to the source) can fix a judge. Add a code-checked genericity test instead of a global novelty rating.

source: Chakrabarty, Laban, Agarwal, Muresan, Wu (2024) Art or Artifice? LLMs and the False Promise of Creativity (TTCW)
finding: Consensual Assessment Technique adapted to writing: 14 binary tests (Fluency, Flexibility, Originality, Elaboration). Experts agree moderately on single tests and well on the total.
numbers: 10 creative writers rated 48 stories (professional vs LLM). Per-test Fleiss kappa 0.41; total pass-count Pearson 0.69. Professional stories passed 84.7% of tests; LLM stories passed 3 to 10 times fewer (GPT-3.5 under 10%, GPT-4 and Claude v1.3 near 30%).
limits: Short stories only. Small number of stories. Models of mid-2023.
agent_relevance: Narrow binary checks plus a count give better rater agreement than one global score. A code-run checklist is a better template than a 1-10 creativity rating.

source: Chakrabarty et al. (2024) TTCW
finding: LLMs asked to administer the same tests (with chain-of-thought) did not agree with experts at all.
numbers: Cohen kappa vs majority of three experts averaged close to zero across 14 tests for GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Claude; GPT-4 exceeded 0.2 on only 2 of 14 tests. Few-shot prompts on a couple of tests gave no significant gain.
quote: none of the LLMs positively correlate with the expert assessments
limits: Zero-shot CoT prompts; few-shot tried on only a couple of tests. Contrasts with positive results on short (<100 words) responses.
agent_relevance: Long-output creativity judging by a model is unreliable even with a decomposed checklist. Judge short outputs, and use code where possible.

source: Chakrabarty et al. (2024) TTCW
finding: Expert comments show how experts tell LLM stories apart: repeated phrases, abrupt endings, weak subtext, simple metaphors. These are surface regularities a program can partly measure.
numbers: Expert free-text rationales (Table 8) cite repeated words and phrases and no use of implication or subtext.
limits: Qualitative, from 10 experts.
agent_relevance: Repetition across drafts and across ideas is detectable in code (n-gram overlap); use it as a cheap reject filter.

source: Zhang, Diddee, Holm et al. (2025) NoveltyBench: Evaluating Language Models for Humanlike Diversity
finding: Measures diversity of repeated samples by counting functionally distinct answers with a trained equivalence classifier. Frontier models give far fewer distinct answers than 8 humans, and larger models are not more diverse.
numbers: distinct_k out of 10 samples: command-r 2.68, Llama-3.3-70B 2.49 vs Llama-3.2-1B 6.74, gemma-2-2b 5.66. DeBERTa classifier 79% accuracy, F1 0.811 on 100 held-out human-labeled pairs; BLEU, ROUGE and BERTScore diverged from human judgment (BERTScore AUC 0.68, DeBERTa 0.81).
limits: Human baseline is 8 paper authors, a low bound on human diversity. Classifier trained on 1,000 pairs. Utility uses a reward model mapped to 0-10.
agent_relevance: Automatic diversity that matches humans: cluster by functional equivalence in code. Embedding cosine and n-gram overlap alone mislead. Related to the paused NoveltyBench run.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) NoveltyBench
finding: Prompt fixes for low diversity: asking for creativity barely helps; showing the model its own earlier outputs works.
numbers: On 100 curated prompts with Claude-3 Opus, GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0 Pro over 8 generations: paraphrasing and system-prompt creativity only marginally effective; in-context regeneration roughly matched human diversity, and GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Pro exceeded human cumulative utility.
quote: asking a model for 'creative outputs' does not work very well
limits: Three models, 8 generations, a 100-prompt subset. Diversity is elicited by prompt, not built in.
agent_relevance: Strong support for archive-conditioned generation (show previous attempts, demand a different one) over generic 'be creative' prompts.

source: Shen, Druckmann, Zou (2026) Unlocking LLM Creativity in Science through Analogical Reasoning
finding: A retrieval-grounded novelty judge: LLM writes queries, Semantic Scholar returns papers, SPECTER embeddings rerank, LLM judges novelty against the top 10. Its agreement with humans is moderate.
numbers: On 98 ideas of the AI Researcher dataset: Spearman 0.358 (median human), 0.411 (mean), 0.427 (min), 0.245 (max); binary accuracy 0.602 to 0.633 for median/mean; mean absolute difference 1.70 vs human-human 1.73 (N=91). Agentic Reviewer reference: human-human rho 0.41, LLM-human 0.42.
limits: Moderate correlation only. The human gold is the same noisy Si et al. ratings. Aggregated-human vs single-pair baseline slightly favours the judge.
agent_relevance: Matches the idea of testing novelty against retrieved prior art. Accuracy is human-level, but human-level is low. Report it as a hint, not a gate.

source: Shen et al. (2026) Analogical Reasoning
finding: A scaffold step (analogy to a far domain) increased judged novelty and diversity, scored by the retrieval judge and by humans.
numbers: Novel solutions over 50% of the time vs as little as 1.6% for baselines; diversity metrics up 90-173%. Human pairwise: AR solution more novel 78% of the time, Cohen kappa 0.445; judged reasonable 67%. About $0.02 per problem. Gemini generated most novel solutions, then GPT, then Claude.
limits: Novelty is defined by the authors' own retrieval judge; the human study had moderate agreement. Four biomedical tasks.
agent_relevance: Links to the analogical-access subfield. Novelty judged by a retrieval step in code plus a model verdict is the pattern we want.

source: Literature-Grounded Novelty Assessment of Scientific Ideas (2025)
finding: Facet-based retrieval (purpose, mechanism, evaluation, domain), SPECTER2 shortlist of 100, LLM rerank to 10, then an LLM novelty verdict with expert examples. Best prompt-only novelty checker in this set.
numbers: 32-item test, gpt-4o: zero-shot accuracy 0.68; with expert examples (idea, papers, class, reasoning) 0.81, F1 0.79, kappa 0.59. AI Scientist checker 0.47 (kappa 0.05); AI Researcher GPT-4o 0.78 (kappa 0.52), Claude-3.5-Sonnet 0.56 (kappa 0.19). Expert agreement on the formative set kappa 0.64 (3 classes), 0.68 (2 classes). Ablation, accuracy on not-novel ideas: full 89.66%, generic-relevance rerank 13.79%, keyword retrieval only 5.17%.
limits: Read via a page-fetch summary, not the PDF text. Only 67 labeled ideas (32 test): one item moves accuracy 3 points. The same annotators wrote the examples and labeled the test items.
agent_relevance: Retrieval quality is the lever, not the judge prompt. Invest in the retrieval and rerank step.

source: Automated Creativity Evaluation of Language Models Across Open-Ended Tasks (2026)
finding: Separates divergent creativity (semantic entropy over clustered continuations, no reference answers) from convergent creativity (retrieval-based multi-agent judge). The two are only weakly related.
numbers: 50 MacGyver problems: semantic entropy vs human Cohen kappa 0.56; cosine 0.49; Distinct-1 0.37; Self-BLEU 0.35. Convergent judge accuracy 84.7% on MacGyver vs ChatEval 76.7%, single GPT-4o prompts 64.7-67.3%, human annotators 80.0-84.7%; BookMIA 83.0%. Novelty judge Spearman 0.80 vs human on 30 solutions. About 63% fewer tokens than ChatEval.
limits: Read via a page-fetch summary; the last third was not read. No human validation on HypoGen. Judge priors can mark unusual viable solutions infeasible.
agent_relevance: A retrieval-grounded judge can reach human-level accuracy on feasibility, while novelty is measured separately without a judge. Fits G5: measure diversity in code.

source: Automated Creativity Evaluation of Language Models Across Open-Ended Tasks (2026)
finding: Thinking mode and model size raise judged convergent creativity; variety does not rise with size.
numbers: MacGyver overall: Vicuna 7B 0.217, Llama 3.1 8B 0.266, GPT-4o 0.63, Llama 3.1 405B 0.51; Qwen3 32B thinking 0.517 vs 0.436 non-thinking; DeepSeek-R1 distilled 70B 0.468 vs Llama 3.3 70B 0.391. Semantic entropy flat or lower with size (Vicuna 7B 2.19, Llama 405B 2.08).
limits: Page-fetch summary; scores come from the authors' own judge.
agent_relevance: Thinking helps usefulness, not variety; variety must be forced by the scaffold (sampling, archive).

source: Measuring LLM Novelty As The Frontier Of Original And High-Quality Output (2025)
finding: Automatic novelty metric: harmonic mean of originality (share of 4-6-grams absent from the training corpus) and quality (LLM judge). Rare nonsense and fluent memorised text both score low.
numbers: Three Upwork annotators, 100 items per task: Krippendorff alpha 0.68 (CoPoet), 0.64 (MacGyver), 0.59 (TinyStories). Best judge o3-mini averaged over 5 runs: Spearman 0.50, 0.52, 0.52 with human mean; Claude 3.7 Sonnet single run 0.38, 0.35, 0.38.
limits: Page-fetch summary. Needs indexed training data, so only open-data models. Exact n-gram matches miss paraphrase. Quality is integer 0-5.
agent_relevance: Averaging 5 judge runs raised correlation by about 0.14; cheap variance reduction. The harmonic mean is a simple code rule that pairs novelty with usefulness (Boden and Ritchie style).

source: Measuring LLM Novelty As The Frontier Of Original And High-Quality Output (2025)
finding: Prompt tricks for novelty trade quality for originality, and novelty is U-shaped in temperature.
numbers: Asking for novelty, novel in-context examples and denial prompting had small effects, often higher originality at lower quality; on MacGyver they could produce degenerate output. Instruction tuning raised novelty at every size, mostly via quality; some base models were less novel than human references.
limits: Open-data models only (Pythia, OLMo, OLMo-2). Page-fetch summary.
agent_relevance: Prompting for 'novel' mostly buys nonsense; gate any novelty push with a usefulness check.

source: The Unlikely Duel: Evaluating Creative Writing in LLMs through a Unique Scenario (2024)
finding: A single unseen prompt (to avoid training contamination), 10 blind raters, 12 LLMs and 5 human writers, 10-item rubric. Top LLMs matched humans overall; humans stayed ahead on creativity and originality.
numbers: Weighted Cohen kappa 0.48 (95% CI 0.43-0.54) between raters; GPT-4 best overall; humor hardest (mean 3.4); each rater scored 13 stories; 5 runs per model.
limits: Page-fetch summary. One prompt, tiny human sample, no LLM judge used.
agent_relevance: Use a fresh unpublished prompt to avoid contamination when comparing creativity; expect rater kappa near 0.5 even with trained raters.

source: Franceschelli and Musolesi (2024) Creative Beam Search: LLM-as-a-Judge for Improving Response Generation
finding: Generate with diverse beam search, then let the same LLM pick the most creative of K=4 candidates. Users preferred it to plain sampling, but the self-judge step was not shown to help.
numbers: 31 graduate students, 217 answers: CBS preferred 45%, standard sampling 29%, too similar 26%. Overlap of the self-judge pick with the diversity-beam pick 29%, below the 35.3% a random pick would give.
limits: Small sample, user-chosen prompts, 256-token outputs. No control that isolates the judge step on user preference. Authors state self-evaluation reflects model priors, not belief.
agent_relevance: A direct example of a creativity judge inside a generation loop. Shows the pattern, not that the judge helps. Supports using code selection (G5).

source: Koivisto and Grassini (2023) Best humans still outperform artificial intelligence in a creative divergent thinking task (news summary only)
finding: On the Alternate Uses Task, three chatbots scored higher than the average human on both semantic distance and human-rated creativity, but the best humans matched or beat them.
numbers: 256 humans vs ChatGPT-3, ChatGPT-4, Copy.Ai on four objects. Semantic distance 0.95 (chatbots) vs 0.91 (humans); creativity rating 2.91 vs 2.47 on a 1-5 scale.
limits: Seen only in a news summary; the paper was not opened.
agent_relevance: Both measures reward the model's mean. For idea generation the tail matters, so compare best-of-n, not means.

source: Organisciak, Acar, Dumas, Berthiaume (2023) Beyond semantic distance: Automated scoring of divergent thinking greatly improves with large language models (project page only)
finding: Fine-tuned LLMs (Ocsai) scored divergent-thinking originality better than embedding semantic distance.
numbers: Project pages state up to r = .81 with human raters; best case, authors' own figure.
limits: Only the project landing page and search snippets were seen; the paper was not opened.
agent_relevance: A model fine-tuned on human ratings of short responses can reach good agreement; a prompt-only judge was not shown to do the same. Open: test on our own rated set.

source: S-DAT (2025) A Multilingual, GenAI-Driven Framework for Automated Divergent Thinking Assessment
finding: Embedding-distance score: average pairwise dissimilarity of 10 words (Divergent Association Task), made multilingual. It correlates weakly with human originality ratings.
numbers: S-DAT vs AUT originality r = .17 (study 1a, n 138-141), .24 (1b, n 205-284), .13 (study 2, up to 8,498); original DAT .32, .32, .13. Bridge-the-Associative-Gap r = .11 and .08 (not significant). Human AUT originality interrater r = .66 in Study 2.
limits: Page-fetch summary. Validation used English data only. Captures novelty by distance, not appropriateness; adversarial gaming not tested.
agent_relevance: Pure embedding distance explains little of rated originality (r about 0.1-0.3). Do not use distance alone as the novelty gate; pair it with retrieval or a usefulness check.

source: Synthesis by this agent across c01-c31 (not a source)
finding: Best agreement with human novelty or creativity ratings tops out near rho 0.4-0.5 for retrieval or judge methods and kappa 0.5-0.6 for expert pairs. Model verdicts without retrieval are near chance on ideas and long stories.
numbers: Humans: kappa 0.41 per test (TTCW), 56.1% top/bottom (Si), 60% (RQ-Bench), kappa 0.48 (Unlikely Duel). Judges: rho 0.36-0.43 (Shen), 0.50-0.52 (n-gram + o3-mini 5-run mean), kappa 0.59 (literature-grounded, 32 items), macro-F1 17.2 (RINoBench), kappa near 0 (TTCW).
limits: Loose comparison: different tasks, scales, golds and sample sizes.
agent_relevance: Keep a judge only if its agreement with a rated set beats the human-human floor on our own task; otherwise use code checks, retrieval distance and execution.
